BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, the game design document, 34 terms for a design that an engineer can build from and a tester can check from its sections and tags to the ways it goes wrong. The exact terms let you tell an AI agent what to write.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Liam in For Bear. Newcomers often treat a GDD, the game design document, as a story about the game. It is not. It is a promise that other people and agents can build from a check with every claim tagged and every test linked. This film goes through its terms group by group, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.

BDEFS.heard: Six labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. In the book text, the course text uses and explains the term. In the glossary, the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it. Computed, the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Simulation, a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game. Illustrative data, numbers chosen to show the idea not measured. Conceptual, a drawing of the idea. With no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map, 34 terms about the GDD, the game design document, and four groups. A GDD is a promise that other people and agents can build from a check. The first group is the documents, the GDD, game brief, pitch, reverse, draft, and gate.

B0102.heard: The second group is what the design says. 16 sections, design pillar, corloop, PX goal, the player experience goal, mechanic scope, out of scope, scope creep, and cut, defer, swap. These terms are what a GDD commits to.

B0103.heard: The third group is linking and checking. Stable ID, a fixed identifier and linked test, then the tags observed inferred missing an assumption then acceptance criterion, given when then tolerance direct state right, invariant, and false pass. These terms say how a claim points at its evidence.

B0104.heard: The fourth group is Seven Ways a GDD Goes Wrong. Ghost Center, Mechanic Mirage, Implementation Void, Priority Inflation, Novelists Trap, Completeness Fallacy, and Stagnant Artifact. These are the Failure Modes a Review Looks for.

B0201.heard: Three bars drawn to length. The top one is the GDD. It says what the game is and how it plays in enough detail that an engineer can build it and a tester can check it. This one is a real recovered GDD of 4777 words. The brief agrees the task and the GDD details it. For example, a GDD for your platformer gives the robot's jump height and meters so a test can measure the jump.

B0202.heard: The red bar is the game brief. It says what the player does, what success is, what can go wrong and what is left out. Its reader is the team and its job is to agree the task and its limits. In this made-up example it runs to 600 words. For example, a brief for a coin game says, collect every coin before time runs out, falling off the level loses and multiplayer is out.

B0203.heard: The short gray bar is the pitch, a short sales description of the game idea. Its reader is someone you want to persuade and it does not have to be buildable yet. Here the made up pitch is 150 words and the GDD is about 32 times as long. For example, a pitch for a robot platformer sells the thrill of the chase and the hunt for coins and gives an engineer nothing to build yet.

B0301.heard: A diagram of game files feeding into a GDD. Reverse means recovering a GDD from a game that already exists. The agent reads the scripts and scenes, and every claim it writes carries a tag that says how it is known. This real one has 107 observed claims, 29 inferred and 30 missing. For example, you point the agent a finished platformer, and it records that falling off the level resets the player. Siding the script line, that does it.

B0302.heard: Below it, an idea feeds into a GDD. Draft means writing a GDD from a new idea with no files yet and marking what you assumed. Every gap the agent fills in carries an assumption tag. Reverse starts from the game, draft starts from the idea, and both end in the same 16 sections. For example, you describe a cave game that has no code yet, and every guest number in the draft, such as the jump height, is tagged as an assumption.

B0303.heard: The picture changes to four design phases, vision, systems, world, and scope with a gate after each. A gate is named sign-off after a design phase and only a person signs it. An asylum run all four stay unsigned. When a person answers they are signed in order four or four, the agent asks a person answers the agent records. For example, after the agent drafts your game's vision, you look it over and sign the vision gate before systems work begins.

B0401.heard: A 4x4 grid fills in one tile at a time. The 16 sections are the fixed outline of a GDD, always in the same order, from their data through pillars, core loop, mechanics and world to risks and open questions. A tester can find any decision by its section. For example, to check how your robots' jump should work, a tester opens the mechanics section and to see whether online play is planned the out of scope section.

B0402.heard: The pillars tile is picked out. A design pillar is a core principle that every decision must support. A GDD has only a few and every later section is checked against them. A pillar guides choices while the core loop is what the player repeats. For example, a platformer with the pillar, falling is never a harsh punishment, keeps response quick and drops any feature that would take away much of the player's progress.

B0403.heard: Now the core loop tile is lit. The core loop is the repeated moment to moment cycle the player enjoys and everything else in the design hangs off it. It is an action the player repeats not a principle. For example in a coin platformer the loop is run, jump, grab a coin and run on and a checkpoint exists to keep that loop going after a fall.

B0501.heard: A graph begins with four goals on the left, control, reward, recovery, and clarity in this made-up example. A PX goal is a feeling the player should have, written in plain words and given an ID such as PX01. A PX goal is what the player should feel, and a mechanic is what the player can do. For example, the player feels safe to try a risky jump is a PX goal for a platformer.

B0502.heard: Five mechanics join the goals. A mechanic is a rule governed action in the game, something the player can do that the rules decide. Each one should serve a goal and hear every goal has at least one. Jump and shoot both serve control. For example, a checkpoint pad that moves your respond point when you stand on it is a mechanic and it serves the goal of recovery.

B0503.heard: Now every box carries a label, Px01 to Px04 and M01 to M05. A stable ID is a label that never changes, so a ticket, a test and a playdest note all point at the same thing. For example, a playdest note says M02, coins hard to see, and the agent and the test both know it means the coin mechanic, even after the coins are renamed gems.

B0504.heard: Six tests appear on the right T20 to T25. A link test is a test row that names the mechanic it checks. Follow the lines and six tests cover four of the five mechanics. M03 shoot has no test and because each row names its mechanic, the gap shows. For example, one test row says touch task B before task A and the task ledger does not change and it names M05 task order.

B0601.heard: A bar of tagged claims from a real recovered GDD. The tag observed means the code does this and the tag names the file and line that show it. Here 107 of 166 claims, 64% are observed. A tag is a claim not evidence so open the line. For example, a tag says the player responds after falling off the level and sites a line of the player's script and you open that line to see the reset.

B0602.heard: The middle gray part is inferred. The code strongly implies the claim without stating it, so the tag must give its evidence. 29 of the 166 claims 17% are inferred. For example, coins placed in a trail along a ledge suggest the route the designer meant the player to take, and the GDD says so with the coin positions as its evidence.

B0603.heard: The light gray part is missing. It marks something the code cannot tell you, so nobody should guess it from the files. 30 of the 166 claims 18% are missing. For example, no script in a recovered platformer says who the target player is or how the game is won, so both are tagged missing for a person to decide.

B0604.heard: A second bar shows a draft in this made-up example. Assumption marks a gap the draft filled in, which nobody saw in any code. Here it is 26 of 50 claims, 52 percent, the largest share in the one to watch. Observed means the code does it, and assumption means the draft guessed. For example, a draft for a new game gives its enemies a patrol speed, and that speed stays tagged as an assumption until a person decides it.

B0701.heard: Two boxes of 12 dots each from the same simulated draws. Ghost centers the failure where no vision is locked, so nothing anchors the decisions in each one drifts. With no vision, the dots miss the center by 130 pixels on average, and with a locked vision by 41. For example, a team that never settles whether it's game is a calm exploration or a speed run ends up with slow puzzles in one level and timed races in the next.

B0702.heard: Now four PX goals are tested. A mechanic mirage is a PX goal that is really a feature described in disguise. Two of these add a rope, swing and build a skill tree, name features, not feelings so nobody can tell when the goal is met. The test is whether you can say it without naming a feature. For example, add a double jump as a mirage and the real goal might be, the player feels free in the air.

B0703.heard: This list is the checkpoint pad, mechanic M04. An implementation void is a mechanic with only the happy path written down, the case where all goes right. At first, only walk onto the pad is written. Then the unhappy cases fill in, walking on again resets a fall in the old checks until six of six are written. For example, a locked door that only says the key opens it is a void until it says what happens without the key.

B0801.heard: Fifteen feature tiles and eight turn red as they are tagged core, the tag for what the game cannot do without. Priority inflation means more than 40% of the features are tagged core. Eight of fifteen is fifty three point three percent over the line and when most things are core nothing is. For example, a platformer that tags hat skins, a photo mode and a leaderboard is core beside run and jump has inflated its priorities.

B0802.heard: Two of the core tiles are demoted. Six of 15 is exactly 40%, which is not more than the limit, so it passes. This step is made up arithmetic. Demoting is the fix for priority inflation, deciding that a feature can be cut or deferred. For example, demote the photo mode in the leaderboard to later, and keep run, jump in the checkpoint as core.

B0901.heard: Two cards of sentences made up for this example. The novelists trap a story written for a reader, not for an engineer. The ruined sigh with old grief is pleasant and nobody can build it. On the left one of three sentences is buildable, and on the right all three are. For example, your robot feels lonely in the dark caves gives an engineer nothing, while the cave lights dim as the robot goes deeper gives a lighting task.

B0902.heard: A table of six decisions made up for this example. The completeness fallacy is a GDD full of decisions with no recorded reasoning. It looks complete, yet only two of six decisions say why. Gravity 22 with no reason could be a choice or an accident. For example, if your GDD sets the jump height and never says why, a teammate may change it without knowing a level depends on it.

B0903.heard: Two version timelines over 10 weeks in this made up history with a prototype built at week 5. A stagnant artifact is a GDD with no version history, never revised after a prototype. The top one is revised three times after the prototype, the bottom one zero. For example, play-desting your prototype shows the checkpoints are too far apart, and a living GDD gets a new version that says so, while a stagnant one keeps the old plan.

B1001.heard: A list of six items with their hours in this made-up plan. Scope is everything the project promises to include. Here move and jump coins, enemies, a checkpoint pad, three levels, and a menu add up to 94 of 100 hours. For example, if your scope promises three levels, those three are what you owe, and any extra level is new work that must be agreed first.

B1002.heard: A red box adds the out of scope list. Out of scope is a written list of what will not be built here multiplayer, a mobile port and XR extended reality. It is excluded on purpose, so a request for multiplayer already has an answer. For example, a checkpoint pad's acceptance criterion lists its look and sound, touch, gamepad and any export as out of scope, so nobody expects them in that build.

B1003.heard: Three red items slip in and extra boss skins and a day night cycle. Scope creep is the quiet growth of work beyond what was agreed. Nobody decided to add these and the total is now 130 of 100 hours. Creep is growth nobody agreed to and out of scope is excluded on purpose. For example, an agent asked to fix the jump also adds a wall climb because it seemed nice and nobody approved it.

B1004.heard: Cut to fur, swap are the three ways to handle too much scope. Cut removes a thing, defer post-pones it, and swap replaces it with something smaller. Here the skins are cut, the day night cycle is deferred, and the boss becomes a six-hour minute boss, so the plan is back to 100 of 100 hours. For example, you cut an extra costume, defer online leaderboards until after launch, and swap a flying enemy for one that only walks.

B1101.heard: Six checks for a checkpoint pad with values measured in a real run. An acceptance criterion is a concrete condition that must be true for work to count as done. A stranger could write its test without asking from a quantity in unit, a limit, a time box, and how the state is reached. Here's six of six pass. For example, the robot should feel responsive is a wish, and the robot reaches the pad within 600 frames is a criterion.

B1102.heard: Check 4 rewritten in 3 parts, given when then is a format for a test, a starting state, an action, and an expected result. Given the pad is active and the player stands elsewhere, when reset is held for 5 frames, then the player is within 0.2 meters of the respond point. It measured 0.0882. For example, given the player stands by the last coin when it is touched, then the gold door opens. The player stands by the last coin when it is touched, then the player stands by the last coin.

B1103.heard: A top view of the 0.2 meter limit. A tolerance is the allowed difference between what you expected and what you got. The real result 0.0882 meters lands inside the ring and passes and the made up point at 0.35 fails. The time box counts engine frames 64 of 600. For example, a test of where the robot lands after a jump accepts a small gap from the target instead of an exact match.

B1201.heard: A chart of player height by frame. A direct state right sets a value in code instead of producing it through gameplay. The red line puts the player at minus 30 meters at frame zero, skipping nine frames of falling are made up fall speed. It tests what follows, not whether a player can get there. For example, a test that sets the score straight to the winning total checks the windscreen, but not that the coins can be collected.

B1202.heard: A list of 5 old checks, an invariant is a condition that must stay true throughout whatever else changes. Here movement, jump, a projectile, reset, and a collected coin must all still pass after the checkpoint is added and 5 of 5 still hold. A change that breaks 1 fails. For example, when an agent adds a dash move to your player, the invariant that the old jump test still passes must hold.

B1203.heard: 21 pass lines are printed in two turn red. A false pass is a test that passes though the behavior is wrong. Two of these were skips that still printed pass so only 19 of 21 tested anything. These counts are from a real test session. Weakening a check so it passes is called loosening. For example, a coin test that cannot find the coin skips itself in prints pass proves nothing about coins.

B1301.heard: Each pair sets look alike terms side by side. Reverse starts from a game that exists and most of its claims are tagged observed. Draft starts from an idea and tags its guesses as assumptions. Both arrows end in a GDD.

B1302.heard: A brief is short about 600 words in the made-up case and agrees the task, success and limits. A GDD is long, a real 4,777 words, detailed enough to build and test.

B1303.heard: Observed means the code does it and a file and line show it here line 36 of the player's script falls below minus 12. Assumption is a gap the draft filled in with no file, no line, only a question mark.

B1304.heard: A mechanic is what the player can do, such as jump or shoot an action. A PX goal is what the player should feel, such as feeling and control and experience. Each mechanic should serve a goal.

B1401.heard: A vague request sits above the exact instruction that replaces it with a chart of what it does. Make the GDD complete becomes, fill all 16 sections and tag every claim observed, inferred, missing or assumption. Then every one of 166 claims has a tag.

B1402.heard: Do not make everything a priority becomes, tag no more than 40% of Features Core at most 6 of 15, before 53% after demoting to 40.

B1403.heard: The checkpoint should respond well becomes, return the player within 0.2 meters of the respond point within two frames at a fixed 60 frames per second. Measured in a constructed fixture that sets the player below the fall threshold in code, not by play, 0.0898 meters under the limit.

B1404.heard: Say what we are not doing becomes right in out of scope list, then cut, defer, or swap until the plan fits 100 hours. With creep it was 130, so 30 hours come out.

B1405.heard: Make sure every mechanic is tested becomes, give each test an ID and name its mechanic, and list any mechanic with no test. Six tests and one untested mechanic, M03.

B1501.heard: This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you trust a design document. First, is the vision locked before the other sections are filled? If not, it is a ghost center.

B1502.heard: Second, does every claim carry a tag observed inferred missing or assumption? And did you open the sighted line? A tag is a claim, not evidence.

B1503.heard: Third, does each PX goal link to a mechanic and each mechanic to a test. A mechanic with no link test is a gap.

B1504.heard: Fourth are no more than 40% of the features tagged core. More than that is priority inflation and nothing is really core.

B1505.heard: Fifth, does the out of scope list say what will not be built? A written list gives scope creep something to be measured against.

B1506.heard: 6. Could a stranger test each criterion with a unit, a limit, and a time box. Then say it exactly. Not make it complete, but every claim tagged, every test linked.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap a brief agrees the task and a GDD is detailed enough to build and test. Reverse starts from a game and a draft starts from an idea. A PX goal is what the player feels and mechanic what the player does. Every claim carries a tag and a tag is a claim not evidence. Priority inflation means more than 40% of features tagged core. An acceptance criterion names a quantity, a tolerance and a time box.

BHTF.heard: Quizmy on game design document terms with short game making cases one at a time. Use reverse draft, game brief, PX goal, mechanic observed, assumption, scope creep out of scope and acceptance criterion. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.

BOUT.heard: Key terms the game design document at Nick Bear Brown.
